etymology: From Latin continere — "to hold in."
biblical_def: Self-restraint of bodily desires, especially sexual; the gift Paul speaks of in 1 Corinthians 7:9 ('if they cannot contain'); part of the fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:23 KJV 'temperance').
webster_summary: Self-restraint, especially sexual.
webster_full: Self-restraint, especially in regard to bodily appetites; in the New Testament, both a gift given to some for the celibate life and a discipline asked of all believers in matters of sexual desire.
scriptures: But if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn.
And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate (egkrateuetai) in all things.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace... temperance: against such there is no law.
corruption_summary: Mocked as repression rather than received as Spirit-given strength.
corruption_paragraphs: Continence is not repression — repression is the unbiblical 'just-don't-think-about-it.' Continence is Spirit-given mastery: desires acknowledged, redirected, refused dominion. The fruit of the Spirit includes self-control because the Spirit Himself produces it where He dwells.
usage: Continence is Spirit-fruit, not white-knuckle willpower.
Pray for the gift, not for absence of desire.

etymology: Greek haplous (ἁπλοῦς) — "single, simple, generous," the eye of undivided focus on God.
biblical_def: Jesus' image (Matt 6:22) for the heart whose loyalty is undivided — the single (haplous) eye that fills the body with light, contrasted with the divided heart serving God and mammon.
webster_summary: The undivided heart focused on God alone.
webster_full: Jesus' image in the Sermon on the Mount of an undivided eye that fills the whole body with light; the Greek haplous can mean either 'single' (focused) or 'generous' — both senses applying to the disciple whose loyalty is wholly God's.
scriptures: The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light. But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness.
The light of the body is the eye: therefore when thine eye is single, thy whole body also is full of light.
A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.
corruption_summary: Read as physical eye-care; missing the heart-loyalty Jesus is teaching.
corruption_paragraphs: The single eye is the heart's undivided gaze. Greek haplous is also the word for generous — divided hearts cannot be generous. The single eye and the open hand are the same disposition: God-focused, world-loose.
usage: Pray for the single eye.
Divided hearts cannot be generous.

etymology: From Latin usura — "interest paid for use."
biblical_def: The lending of money at interest to a brother in need; explicitly forbidden in the Mosaic law (Exod 22:25; Lev 25:36-37; Deut 23:19-20) and condemned by the prophets (Ezek 18:8, 13).
webster_summary: Lending at interest to a brother in need.
webster_full: The taking of interest on loans; in the Mosaic law specifically forbidden when lending to a fellow Israelite in need (though permitted with foreigners in commercial transactions); historically extended by the church to all interest-taking, modified in modern times to a distinction between productive lending and oppression of the poor.
scriptures: If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury.
Take thou no usury of him, or increase: but fear thy God; that thy brother may live with thee. Thou shalt not give him thy money upon usury, nor lend him thy victuals for increase.
He that hath not given forth upon usury, neither hath taken any increase, that hath withdrawn his hand from iniquity... he is just.
corruption_summary: Dismissed entirely as ancient law inapplicable to modern finance, missing the principle: do not exploit the poor.
corruption_paragraphs: The Mosaic ban on usury aimed at protecting the poor brother. Modern finance is not all sin — but predatory lending against the desperate is. Payday loans, exploitative credit cards, and aggressive collection agencies fall under the prophetic indictment Ezekiel pronounced. The principle survives: do not profit off your brother's distress.
usage: Lend to the poor without interest.
Predatory lending falls under prophetic judgment.

etymology: From Old English gamen "game" + suffix; the wagering of value on chance.
biblical_def: The wagering of value on chance for personal gain — not addressed by name in Scripture but failing the principles of stewardship, work, contentment, and love of neighbor.
webster_summary: Wagering value on chance for personal gain.
webster_full: The practice of wagering value on outcomes of chance; though not addressed by name in Scripture, fails the biblical principles of work as the proper means of gain, contentment with what God provides, stewardship rather than risk of resources, and love of neighbor (since gambling derives gain from another's loss).
scriptures: Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished: but he that gathereth by labour shall increase.
But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare... For the love of money is the root of all evil.
Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good.
corruption_summary: Defended as harmless entertainment, missing how thoroughly it fails the biblical principles of money.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture does not name gambling as such, but every principle of biblical financial ethics is violated by it: gain comes from labor, not chance; wealth is stewarded, not risked; and the love of neighbor forbids profit from his loss. State-sanctioned lotteries fall in the same indictment.
usage: Earn by labor; do not gain by chance.
Profit on another's loss fails neighbor-love.

etymology: From Old French amuser — originally "to deceive," later "to entertain"; literally "to muse-not."
biblical_def: Diversion or entertainment that distracts from thoughtful engagement; not condemned in itself but dangerous when it becomes the dominant mode of life (Eccl 7:4; 1 Cor 10:7).
webster_summary: Entertainment that diverts from thought.
webster_full: Etymologically 'to muse not' — that which diverts the mind from serious thought; not sinful in itself, but a danger when it becomes the dominant mode of life. The wise heart is not against play but against amusement that displaces wisdom.
scriptures: The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning; but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth.
Neither be ye idolaters, as were some of them; as it is written, The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.
Traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God.
corruption_summary: Industrialized as 'entertainment' that fills every moment, leaving no room for the wisdom-shaping silence Scripture commends.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern entertainment industries make amusement the constant mode. Scripture honors play but warns against amusement as life. The wise heart is not against laughter — it is against laughter that displaces lament. Recover the house of mourning along with the house of mirth.
usage: Limit amusement; recover wisdom-shaping silence.
Both the house of mirth and the house of mourning.

etymology: From Old French leisir "to be permitted," from Latin licere.
biblical_def: Time freed from labor for restoration, worship, and contemplation; the biblical pattern is rhythmic rest within work, climaxing in the Sabbath (Mark 6:31; Heb 4:9-10).
webster_summary: Time freed from labor for restoration and worship.
webster_full: Time freed from labor not for indulgence but for restoration, worship, fellowship, and contemplation; the biblical rhythm is six-and-one (six days work, one day rest) — leisure built into creation order rather than seized as escape.
scriptures: And he said unto them, Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while: for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work.
There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God.
corruption_summary: Reframed as the goal of life ('weekend living') instead of as restorative interlude woven into vocation.
corruption_paragraphs: Leisure for the Bible is not the point of the week — work is. But leisure rightly used (Sabbath, fellowship, worship, rest) makes the work fruitful. Modern life often inverts the order: work is what we endure to fund leisure. Recover six-and-one rhythm.
usage: Build leisure into the week, not at its expense.
Rest is restoration, not escape.

etymology: From Latin punctum "point"; the keeping of appointed time-points.
biblical_def: Keeping appointed times; the practical expression of love-of-neighbor in respect for others' time and of integrity in keeping one's word (Matt 5:37; Eccl 3:1).
webster_summary: Keeping appointed times; respect for others' time.
webster_full: The practical virtue of keeping appointed times; not directly named in Scripture but flowing from the principles of integrity (let your yes be yes), love-of-neighbor (treating others' time as worthy of respect), and the goodness of order (a time for everything).
scriptures: But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: Treated as personality preference, not as ethical practice.
corruption_paragraphs: Punctuality is not a personality trait — it is an ethic. To make others wait is to take their time without consent. Habitual lateness is functional theft. Christians should be marked by the small faithfulness of being where we said we would be when we said we would be there.
usage: Be where you said when you said.
Punctuality is love-of-neighbor with a clock.

etymology: Compound of 'promise' and 'keep,' a deeply biblical character marker.
biblical_def: The faithfulness to fulfill what one has spoken; modeled by God's keeping of His covenant word and commanded of His people (Num 23:19; Ps 15:4; Matt 5:37).
webster_summary: Faithfulness in fulfilling what one has spoken.
webster_full: The character marker of fulfilling what one has spoken; modeled in God's perfect covenant-keeping ('not one word hath failed') and required of His people, including swearing to one's own hurt (Ps 15:4) and letting yes be yes (Matt 5:37).
scriptures: He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay.
God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it?
corruption_summary: Eroded by a culture of fluid commitments — circumstances change, plans change, promises change.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 15 lists swearing-to-one's-own-hurt-and-changing-not as a marker of those who dwell with God. Modern culture treats promises as conditional on convenience. The disciple keeps his word at cost, because his Father keeps His.
roots_summary: Hebrew dabar — word; Greek logos — word.
usage: Swear to your own hurt and change not.
A culture of broken promises produces broken people.

etymology: Compound of oath (Old English ath) and keep.
biblical_def: The fulfillment of oaths sworn before God; an act of fundamental moral seriousness in Scripture (Eccl 5:4-5; Lev 19:12; Num 30:2).
webster_summary: Fulfilling oaths sworn before God.
webster_full: The fulfillment of oaths and vows sworn before God; in Scripture treated with great seriousness — better not to vow than to vow and not pay; the false swearer profanes God's name; oath-keeping is among the marks of the righteous in Psalm 15.
scriptures: When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it... Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.
If a man vow a vow unto the LORD, or swear an oath to bind his soul with a bond; he shall not break his word, he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth.
And ye shall not swear by my name falsely, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God.
corruption_summary: Lost in a culture where contractual fine print is more honored than spoken word.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture takes oaths so seriously Jesus could say 'do not swear at all' and instead let yes mean yes. The culture that needs notarized contracts to enforce its agreements has already lost the moral substance Scripture assumed. Recover the spoken word as binding.
usage: Better not to vow than to vow and break.
Yes means yes.

etymology: Hebrew neder (נֶדֶר) — vow.
biblical_def: Solemn promises made to God, often in the context of distress or thanksgiving, binding the one who vows; not commanded but binding once made (Num 30; Eccl 5:4-5).
webster_summary: Solemn promises made to God, binding once made.
webster_full: Solemn promises made to God, often in distress ('if you deliver me, I will...') or thanksgiving; not required but absolutely binding once made; specially regulated by Mosaic law (Numbers 30) and warned about by Ecclesiastes.
scriptures: I will pay my vows unto the LORD now in the presence of all his people.
When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools.
Paul... having shorn his head in Cenchrea: for he had a vow.
corruption_summary: Either dismissed as legalism or made too casually; Scripture's middle path is to vow with great seriousness when one vows.
corruption_paragraphs: Vows are not commanded, but vows once made are binding. Better to commit privately and quietly than to make public vows you cannot keep. The God who keeps every word of His promise expects His people to keep theirs.
usage: Pay your vows.
If you cannot keep, do not make.

etymology: Compound; the failure to fulfill a vow once sworn.
biblical_def: The unfulfilled vow before God — repented of through confession and restoration where possible; a serious matter not to be treated lightly (Lev 5:4-5; Num 30:13-15; Eccl 5:6).
webster_summary: An unfulfilled vow requiring confession and restoration.
webster_full: A vow once sworn but not paid; serious in Scripture's reckoning, requiring confession ('he shall confess') and where possible the trespass offering for cleansing; in marriage, broken vows are still vows that wounded those who trusted.
scriptures: Or if a soul swear, pronouncing with his lips to do evil, or to do good... and he shall be guilty in one of these: And it shall be, when he shall be guilty in one of these things, that he shall confess that he hath sinned.
Suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin; neither say thou before the angel, that it was an error.
Yet she is thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant.
corruption_summary: Treated as ordinary breakage in modern fluid culture; Scripture treats unfulfilled vows with great gravity.
corruption_paragraphs: Marriage covenants, ministry vows, financial commitments, baptismal pledges — all weigh more than modern culture treats them. When broken, the path forward is confession, restoration where possible, and grace through the cross. The remedy is not to pretend the vow did not exist.
usage: Confess broken vows; do not pretend.
Restoration where possible; grace where not.

etymology: From Latin reparare "to make ready again, repair."
biblical_def: Practical making-amends for wrong done — restoring property, paying restitution, repairing relationships; required in the Mosaic trespass offering (Lev 6:1-7) and exemplified by Zacchaeus (Luke 19:8).
webster_summary: Practical making-amends for wrong done.
webster_full: The practical making-amends for harm done — restoring stolen property, paying restitution plus a fifth in the Mosaic trespass offering, and acting upon Christ's principle 'first be reconciled to thy brother.' Zacchaeus exemplifies it: 'if I have taken any thing... I restore him fourfold.'
scriptures: He shall even restore it in the principal, and shall add the fifth part more thereto, and give it unto him to whom it appertaineth.
And Zacchaeus stood, and said unto the Lord; Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold.
Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.
corruption_summary: Forgotten under cheap-grace theology where forgiveness erases the obligation to make right.
corruption_paragraphs: Forgiveness is free; reparation is owed. The thief who is forgiven still owes restitution. Cheap grace skips this; biblical grace honors it. Zacchaeus modelled the post-conversion ethic: making right what conversion exposed.
usage: Make reparation; do not skip the cost.
Forgiven sin still owes neighbor.

etymology: From Latin conscientia + Old French cler.
biblical_def: The state of integrity Paul names repeatedly — a conscience void of offense toward God and man, kept by repentance and right living (Acts 24:16; 1 Tim 1:5; 3:9; 1 Pet 3:16).
webster_summary: A conscience void of offense toward God and man.
webster_full: The Pauline ideal: a conscience void of offense toward God and toward men, maintained by faith, repentance from known sin, and forthright dealing with neighbors. Required of deacons and ministers; available to every believer through honesty and confession.
scriptures: And herein do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men.
Now the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of faith unfeigned.
Having a good conscience; that, whereas they speak evil of you, as of evildoers, they may be ashamed.
corruption_summary: Replaced by 'positive vibes' or 'no regrets' messaging that bypasses repentance.
corruption_paragraphs: A clear conscience is not the absence of regret — it is the presence of confession-and-cleansing. Paul exercised himself to maintain it. Daily confession, restitution where needed, and ongoing pursuit of righteousness keep the conscience clear. Take the stewardship seriously.
usage: Exercise yourself to keep a clear conscience.
Confession and restitution clean it.

etymology: From Old English gylt; the moral verdict of having actually offended God or neighbor.
biblical_def: The objective moral state of having broken God's law, distinguished from feelings of guilt (true or false); the state to which the gospel responds with real forgiveness (Rom 3:19; 1 John 1:9).
webster_summary: Objective state of having broken God's law.
webster_full: The objective moral state of having actually broken God's law — guilt before God, regardless of whether subjectively felt; distinguished from neurotic false guilt (feeling guilty for what is not actual sin) and from absent guilt (not feeling what is actually owed). Only true guilt is forgiven by the cross.
scriptures: Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight.
corruption_summary: Therapy culture pathologizes all guilt as toxic; Scripture distinguishes true guilt (which leads to repentance) from false guilt (which does not).
corruption_paragraphs: Therapy can confuse the picture: not all guilt is neurotic. True guilt is the soul's right reaction to actual sin. The gospel handles true guilt by forgiving it; therapy alone cannot remove what only Christ can. Distinguish the kinds; receive the cross for what is actually owed.
usage: Distinguish true guilt from false.
True guilt only the cross removes.

etymology: Theological category drawn from 2 Corinthians 7:10 and Ezekiel's call to remember and be ashamed.
biblical_def: The painful awareness of having failed God or neighbor that drives toward repentance and life — distinguished from worldly shame which drives to despair (2 Cor 7:9-10; Ezek 16:63).
webster_summary: Pain at sin that drives to repentance and life.
webster_full: The proper, sanctifying response of conscience to sin — painful awareness that drives toward confession, repentance, and life; Paul's 'godly sorrow' that worketh repentance to salvation; distinguished from worldly shame that drives to hiding, despair, and death.
scriptures: For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.
That thou mayest remember, and be confounded, and never open thy mouth any more because of thy shame, when I am pacified toward thee.
O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to thee, my God: for our iniquities are increased over our head.
corruption_summary: Banished entirely under therapeutic frameworks; Scripture prescribes godly shame as part of repentance.
corruption_paragraphs: The age has banished shame; Scripture distinguishes it. Godly shame is repentance's first step — Ezra blushes before he prays. The cure for godly shame is the gospel's mercy, not the absence of feeling. Reclaim shame as servant of repentance.
usage: Receive godly shame as repentance's first step.
The gospel turns shame into mercy.

etymology: Modern psychological category contrasted with biblical 'godly sorrow.'
biblical_def: The condemning, identity-destroying false shame that says 'I am wrong' rather than 'I did wrong'; not sanctified by Scripture but absorbed by Christ at the cross (Heb 12:2; Rom 8:1).
webster_summary: False, identity-destroying shame absorbed at the cross.
webster_full: The false, identity-destroying shame that condemns the self rather than the sin — saying 'I am bad' rather than 'I did bad'; not from God; absorbed by Christ who 'endured the cross, despising the shame'; replaced for the believer by 'no condemnation.'
scriptures: Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame.
There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.
For your shame ye shall have double; and for confusion they shall rejoice in their portion.
corruption_summary: Confused with godly shame, leaving Christians paralyzed under condemnation Christ already bore.
corruption_paragraphs: Toxic shame says: you are damaged goods. The gospel says: He despised the shame for joy of bringing you home. Distinguish toxic from godly. Bring godly shame to the cross for repentance; bring toxic shame to the cross to leave it there permanently.
usage: Bring toxic shame to the cross to leave it.
Christ despised it; do not carry what He bore.

etymology: Compound; the disciplined ordering of one's own life under God.
biblical_def: The ordering of one's own appetites, time, words, and habits under God's lordship; the Spirit-given fruit of self-control rendered in deliberate practice (1 Cor 9:27; 2 Tim 1:7).
webster_summary: Spirit-given ordering of one's own appetites and habits.
webster_full: The deliberate practice of ordering one's own life — appetites, time, words, habits — under God's lordship; the practical outworking of the Spirit's gift of self-control; required of athletes (1 Cor 9), ministers, and all believers.
scriptures: But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.
For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind (sōphronismos — self-discipline).
Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world.
corruption_summary: Reframed as self-help instead of received as Spirit-empowered obedience.
corruption_paragraphs: Self-discipline without the Spirit is white-knuckle religion. Self-discipline with the Spirit is glad obedience. The Christian doesn't deny himself out of self-loathing but out of love for the One who first loved him. Means and motive matter.
usage: Discipline the body; don't be a castaway.
Spirit-power, not white knuckles.

etymology: From Latin restringere — "to bind back."
biblical_def: The disposition of holding-back from evil — from speech, from action, from indulgence; one of the marks of wisdom (Prov 10:19; 17:27).
webster_summary: The wise disposition of holding-back.
webster_full: The disposition that holds back from evil speech, hasty action, sinful indulgence; the brake of wisdom on the engine of impulse; especially praised in Proverbs concerning the tongue and in the Pastoral Epistles concerning leaders.
scriptures: In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise.
He that hath knowledge spareth his words: and a man of understanding is of an excellent spirit.
But the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer.
corruption_summary: Mocked as inhibition or repression; Proverbs honors it as wisdom.
corruption_paragraphs: The age tells you to express everything; Proverbs honors the one who restrains. Not all impulses are healthy; not all words are useful; not all desires are right. The disposition to hold back is one of wisdom's chief markers — the brake the wise heart has built in.
usage: Refrain your lips and be wise.
Restraint is the brake of wisdom.

etymology: From Greek empatheia — "feeling in," not directly biblical but available as a category.
biblical_def: The capacity to enter into another's experience — modeled by Christ who 'took our infirmities' and 'was touched with the feeling of our infirmities' (Heb 4:15; Matt 8:17); not a master virtue but a servant of love and truth.
webster_summary: Capacity to enter another's experience.
webster_full: The capacity to enter into another's experience — feeling-with rather than feeling-for. Modeled by Christ who took our infirmities and is touched with the feeling of them. Biblical empathy serves love and truth; it is not autonomous, and it never overrides righteousness.
scriptures: For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.
Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.
And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it.
corruption_summary: Elevated to master virtue, eclipsing truth and discipline; biblical empathy serves love and never overrides righteousness.
corruption_paragraphs: Empathy unanchored from truth becomes sentimental enabling. The age says 'just be empathetic'; Scripture binds empathy to love-and-truth. Christ wept at the tomb but also drove out the moneychangers. Same heart; different occasions. Empathy without discipline is incomplete love.
usage: Weep with those who weep.
Empathy serves truth; it does not replace it.

etymology: From Greek sympatheia — "suffering together."
biblical_def: The fellow-feeling of another's pain that prompts compassionate response; modeled by Christ as our high priest who is 'touched with the feeling of our infirmities' (Heb 4:15; 1 Pet 3:8).
webster_summary: Fellow-feeling of another's pain prompting response.
webster_full: The fellow-feeling that arises in observing another's pain or distress, prompting compassionate response; modeled by Christ our high priest who 'was touched with the feeling of our infirmities'; commanded among believers in 1 Peter 3:8.
scriptures: For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities.
Finally, be ye all of one mind, having compassion one of another (sympatheis), love as brethren, be pitiful, be courteous.
corruption_summary: Treated as weakness or condescension; Scripture treats it as the heart of Christ-like ministry.
corruption_paragraphs: Sympathy is not pity-from-above; it is suffering-with-from-alongside. Christ does not look down on our infirmities; He shares them. Recover sympathy as participation in another's experience, not management of it from a distance.
usage: Sympathy is suffering-with, not management.
Christ as our sympathizing High Priest.

etymology: From Latin honestas "honor, respectability"; Greek timios — honorable.
biblical_def: The character of truthfulness in word and integrity in deed — refusing the false weight, the false report, the false witness; required by the law and reaffirmed by Christ (Lev 19:35-36; Rom 12:17; 2 Cor 8:21).
webster_summary: Truthfulness in word and integrity in deed.
webster_full: The integrated character of truthful speech and upright action; refusing false weights, false witness, and false report; providing 'things honest' before God and men; the character grace produces and the law demanded.
scriptures: Recompense to no man evil for evil. Provide things honest in the sight of all men.
Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men.
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
corruption_summary: Reduced to 'not lying' rather than the integrated character Scripture portrays — true word and true deed together.
corruption_paragraphs: Biblical honesty is wider than not-lying. It is true weights, true reports, true testimony, true work. Lev 19 binds them all together. The Christian's whole conduct is to be honest before God and man — not merely his words.
usage: Provide things honest in everyone's sight.
True words; true weights; true work.

etymology: From Latin sincerus "unmixed, pure"; perhaps from sine cera "without wax" (unfilled).
biblical_def: Purity of motive — unmixed, undisguised, free from the fillers of pretense; required of preaching (2 Cor 2:17), of love (1 Pet 1:22), and of life (Phil 1:10).
webster_summary: Purity of motive; unmixed, undisguised heart.
webster_full: Purity of motive — unmixed with self-interest, undisguised, free from the wax-filled cracks of pretense; required of preaching ('not... handling the word of God deceitfully'), of love ('unfeigned love of the brethren'), and of conduct generally.
scriptures: For we are not as many, which corrupt the word of God: but as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God speak we in Christ.
Seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit unto unfeigned love of the brethren.
That ye may be sincere and without offence till the day of Christ.
corruption_summary: Reduced to 'meaning what you say' instead of the deeper purity of motive Scripture demands.
corruption_paragraphs: Sincerity is more than meaning what you say. It is meaning what you say without filler — without ulterior motive, without pretense, without performance. Etymology helps: sine cera, without wax. Sculptors filled cracks with wax to fake quality. Christians don't fill character cracks with religious wax.
usage: No wax in the cracks.
Sincere love; sincere word; sincere life.

etymology: From Old English fæðful + -ness; Hebrew emunah — steadiness, faithfulness.
biblical_def: Reliable steadfastness over time — God's primary character toward His covenant (Lam 3:23) and the character He produces in His people (Gal 5:22; 1 Cor 4:2).
webster_summary: Reliable steadfastness over time.
webster_full: The character of being reliable, trustworthy, steady over time; God's primary covenant attribute and the corresponding character He produces in His people through the Spirit; especially required of stewards (1 Cor 4:2) and elders.
scriptures: It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith (faithfulness).
Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
corruption_summary: Reduced to belief or conviction; biblical faithfulness is sustained reliability across decades.
corruption_paragraphs: Faithfulness in Scripture is decade-long, not moment-long. The Lord's compassions are 'new every morning' — that is faithfulness. The faithful steward is the one found at his post when the master returns. Plodding faithfulness is the spectacular virtue.
usage: Plodding faithfulness is spectacular.
Be found faithful.

etymology: From Old English; KJV translation of Greek tapeinophrosynē — humility of mind.
biblical_def: The mind that takes a low place — Christ's pattern in Philippians 2:3-8 — esteeming others, refusing self-promotion, taking the form of a servant.
webster_summary: The mind that takes a low place.
webster_full: The Pauline term for humility — literally 'low-mindedness' — esteeming others above oneself, refusing self-promotion, taking the form of a servant; Christ's pattern in Philippians 2 by which He emptied Himself.
scriptures: Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
I therefore... beseech you that ye walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called, with all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering.
Serving the Lord with all humility of mind, and with many tears.
corruption_summary: Mistaken for self-deprecation or low self-esteem; biblical lowliness is honest self-knowledge plus active esteem of others.
corruption_paragraphs: Lowliness is not thinking less of yourself; it is thinking of yourself less, and thinking of others as worth Christ's death — because they are. Christ in Philippians 2 was not down on Himself; He was up on us. Lowliness is the Christ-shape of love.
usage: Esteem others better than yourselves.
Christ-shaped lowliness, not self-loathing.

etymology: From Latin contentus "satisfied," from continere.
biblical_def: The settled satisfaction with what God has provided that Paul calls great gain (1 Tim 6:6); learned through experience and Spirit-power, not native to the heart (Phil 4:11-13).
webster_summary: Settled satisfaction with what God provides.
webster_full: The settled satisfaction with what God has provided — neither idleness nor consumerism — that Paul calls 'great gain'; learned through experience in want and abundance; the Spirit-empowered freedom from envy and grasping.
scriptures: I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content... I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.
But godliness with contentment is great gain... having food and raiment let us be therewith content.
Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
corruption_summary: Replaced by perpetual aspirational restlessness; the consumer engine cannot run on contented hearts.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern marketing depends on discontent. Christianity teaches contentment as great gain. The two are at war. Paul learned contentment in want and in abundance — both are contexts for the lesson. Begin by giving thanks for what you already have.
usage: Godliness with contentment is great gain.
Learn contentment in want and abundance both.
